patient_note_history:
History
HPI: A 53-year-old male complains of intermittent dizziness x 2 days. There is a sensation of the room spinning around him. It isn't specific to time and usually occurs when getting up or lying down. The episodes last 20-30 minutes and are progressively getting worse. He has left-sided hearing loss since yesterday. The patient also complains of nausea and vomiting. He had nonbloody diarrhea x 3 days that has since resolved. There is no tinnitus, fullness in the ear, ear discharge, headache, or head trauma. There is no recent URI.
ROS: Negative except as above.
Allergies: NKDA.
Medications: Furosemide, captopril.
PMH: Hypertension, diagnosed 7 years ago.
PSH: Appendectomy.
SH: No smoking, 2-3 beers/week, no illicit drugs.
FH: Noncontributory.

exam_lines.source_text: Patient is in no acute distress.
VS: Within normal limits, no orthostatic changes.

HEENT: Normocephalic/atn atraumatic, pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation, extraocular movements intact without nystagmus, no papilledema, no cerumen, tympanic membranes normal, mouth and oropharynx normal.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, heart sounds within normal limits; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.

Neuro: Cranial nerves 2-12 grossly intact except for decreased hearing acuity in the left ear. Normal Rinne (air conduction > bone conduction on the left), Weber right lateralization, 8 Dix-Hallpike maneuver. Motor: Strength 5/5 throughout. Deep tendon reflexes: 2+ intact, symmetric, Babinski sign bilaterally. Cerebellar: Normal Romberg, finger-to-nose normal. Gait: Normal.

gold_target:
Diagnosis #1: Ménière's disease
History Finding(s):
- Sensation of room spinning
Physical Exam Finding(s):
- Decreased hearing acuity on the left
- Episodic left-sided hearing loss
- Normal Rinne test

Diagnosis #2: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
History Finding(s):
- Sensation of room spinning
- Onset with positional changes
- Duration 2D-30 minutes
Physical Exam Finding(s): None provided

Diagnosis #3: Orthostatic hypotension causing dizziness
History Finding(s):
- History of diarrhea
- Taking antihypertensive medication
Physical Exam Finding(s): None provided
gold_additional_diagnosis:
• Labyrinthitis: This frequently follows a viral infection (usually a URI) and is accompanied by hearing loss and tinnitus, but vertigo is usually continuous and lasts several days to a week.
• Perilymphatic fistula: This is a rare cause of vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss that usually results from head trauma or extensive barotrauma. Episodes of vertigo are fleeting, generally lasting seconds.
• Acoustic neuroma: Acoustic neuroma more commonly causes continuous disequilibrium rather than episodic vertigo. As noted above, central lesions are unlikely in patients with vertigo, hearing loss, and an otherwise normal neurologic exam. However, an intracranial mass lesion must be ruled out in any patient with unilateral hearing loss.
• Hypotension due to volume depletion/electrolyte imbalance: Since the patient has vomiting and watery diarrhea, and is also on a diuretic, she may be volume-depleted.
raw_opening:
Opening Scenario:

Edward Albright, a 53-year-old male, comes to the emergency department (ED) complaining of dizziness.

Vital Signs:

BP: 135/90 mm Hg 
Temp: 98.0°F (36.7°C) 
RR: 16/minute 
HR: 76/minute, regular 
Cranial nerves, motor exam, DTRs, gait, Romberg sign, Dix-Hallpike maneuver

Examinee Tasks:

1. Take a focused history.
2. Perform a focused physical exam (do not perform rectal, genitourinary, or female breast exam).
3. Explain your clinical impression and workup plan to the patient.
4. Write the patient note after leaving the room.

Checklist/SP Sheet:

Patient Description:

Patient - a 53-year-old male, married with three children.

Notes for the SP:

- Ask the examinee to speak loudly. Pretend that you have difficulty hearing in your left ear and that you hear better when the examinee moves closer to your right ear.
- Refuse to walk if the examinee asks you to. Pretend that you are afraid of falling down. Walk only if the examinee explains why he/she would like to see your gait.

Challenging Questions to Ask:

"I'm quite anxious about my hearing, doctor. Do you believe this condition will be permanent?"

Examinee Response:

"I understand your concern, Mr. Albright. Several permanent and transient conditions may be responsible for your symptoms. However, to provide a more definitive answer, I would like to conduct additional tests to clarify the reasons behind your dizziness and auditory issues.. After that, we can discuss possible reasons for your hearing problems."

Examinee Checklist:

Entrance:

- Examinee knocked on the door before entering.
- Examinee made eye contact with the SP.
- Examinee correctly used the patient's name.
- Examinee introduced self by name.
- Examinee identified his/her role or position.

Reflective Listening:

- Examinee asked an open-ended question and actively listened to the response.
- Examinee asked the SP to list his/her concerns and listened to the response without interrupting.
- Examinee summarized the SP's concerns, often using the SP's own words.

Information Gathering:

- Examinee elicited data efficiently and accurately.

Connecting With the Patient:

- Examinee recognized the SP's emotions and responded with PEARLS.

Patient: "No."

Physical Examination:

- Examinee washed their hands.
- Examinee asked permission to start the exam.
- Examinee used respectful draping.
- Examinee did not repeat painful maneuvers.

Exam Component Maneuvers:

- HEENT: Inspected for nystagmus, tympanic membrane, otoscopic exam for hearing assessment, Rinne and Weber tests, inspected mouth and throat.
- CV exam: Auscultation, orthostatic vital signs.
- Neurologic exam: Cranial nerves, motor exam, deep tendon reflexes, gait, Romberg sign, Dix-Hallpike maneuver.

Sample Closure:

"Mr. Albright, your dizziness could stem from an issue with your ears or brain, or it might be caused by low blood pressure.. We will have to run some tests to pinpoint the source of your symptoms. This will involve blood tests, a hearing assessment, and an MRI that will deliver precise images of your brain.. Until we find the cause of your problem, you should be careful when you stand up quickly or walk unaccompanied, and you should use hand railings whenever possible. Do you have any questions for me?"

Closure:

- Examinee discussed initial diagnostic impressions.
- Examinee discussed initial management plans.
- Follow-up tests.
